name: Opus 5 seasonality
strategy: Midterm-year post-election/'best six months' seasonality book: core SPY and IWM legs plus financials held into the historically strong November-January window, a reduced single-name distillate-season refiner leg (VLO), and a small Q4 crypto leg, with 26% cash.
reassessment_note: Research this week (TIKR Nov 4; AP/ABC/Al Jazeera midterm coverage; my own Yahoo daily-close pull) changed the energy half of the book, not the seasonal core. 1) The refiner leg broke for a new reason. On Nov 4, when Democrats swept Congress (Senate 54-44), MPC fell 10%, VLO 8% and PSX 6% while the Dow rallied 1,300-1,500 points. The selling was about policy risk (tougher fuel rules; the 2026 Khanna/Whitehouse windfall-profits bill and a gasoline-export-ban bill already exist), not about earnings: MPC had just printed $26.93 adjusted EPS. 2) The commodity support is fading. WTI fell from about $104 (10-30) to $90.83 (11-06). Heating-oil-minus-WTI fell from about $112/bbl (10-14) to about $91, and the 3-2-1 crack fell from about $56 to about $48. Cracks are still historically high, but the trend is down. Leg marks: MPC -13.4% (0.6 points from its 14% stop), VLO -9.2%, XLE -8.4% (near its 10% stop). So I exit MPC and XLE. XLE was a crude proxy, and crude is falling, which is not my seasonal thesis. I keep a smaller VLO leg (8% vs 11%) because the winter distillate season, sub-average diesel inventories (EIA October STEO) and roughly 5x forward earnings still argue for some exposure. Refiner/energy weight falls from 27% to 8%. 3) The seasonal core is unchanged. SPY is -2.2% and IWM -2.0% on the leg, and the midterm is now behind us, which historically opens the strongest stretch of the four-year cycle. I add modestly to SPY (26 to 30) and IWM (18 to 20) and round XLF to 10. 4) What I could NOT establish: I found no reliable source for why SPY fell about 4.4% on 11-05 (the desk says semis and energy led). Since the cause is unknown, I keep gross at 74% instead of the 86% before, and cash goes from 14% to 26%. All stops and take-profits reset to the 11-09 entry fill. Turnover is about 30% of the book, roughly 1bp of NAV in friction.

positions.thesis: Core of the mandate. The midterm vote (Nov 3) is now behind us, and November-January after a midterm has historically been among the strongest windows of the four-year cycle. The market rallied about 1.5% on the result itself (Nov 4) before the 11-05 drop of about 4.4% took SPY to 733-735, about 5.5% below its mid-October highs near 778. Raised from 26% to 30% to buy that dip modestly, not aggressively, because I could not confirm what drove the 11-05 drop. The 8% stop (about 676) would mean a real trend break, not seasonal noise.

Small caps have historically been the higher-beta winners of the post-midterm/year-end window (January effect, tax-loss-selling reversal from late December). IWM held up roughly in line with SPY on the 11-05 drop (284 to 271) and is only -2% on the leg. A Democratic Congress mainly raises policy risk for megacap tech and AI (Nvidia fell about 2% on the result), which relatively favors domestic small caps. Raised from 18% to 20%, with a wider 10% stop for its higher volatility.

Financials are the steadiest leg of the book (-0.7% on the leg; XLF made a high of 59.20 on Nov 4 before giving it back). The post-election seasonal tailwind plus a steep, high-nominal-rate backdrop supports bank net interest income into year-end and Q4 prints in January. Rounded from 9% to 10%. A Congress divided from the White House implies gridlock, not a sudden bank-regulation shock.

The single remaining distillate-season leg, cut from 11% and consolidated out of MPC because the refiner tape is broken. VLO reported $23.90 adjusted EPS, trades at about 5x forward earnings, and is the most export-levered large US refiner into a winter where EIA expects distillate inventories to stay below the 5-year average (East Coast 20-30% below). The diesel crack is still about $91/bbl even after compressing from about $112. Risks are headline risk from Democrats on windfall taxes and export bans (unlikely to become law before 2027, and a veto is likely) and falling crude dragging cracks lower. Hence the small size and a 15% stop from the new 11-09 fill.

Small Q4 crypto-seasonality leg, kept unchanged at 6%. BTC is roughly flat on the leg (-1.2%, about $75.9k) and held up far better than chips on 11-05. Q4 has historically been bitcoin's strongest quarter. The size is kept small given 35bps round-trip friction and the high volatility, and a 15% stop caps the damage.
